## Data

```{python}
# create the data folders if they don't exist
os.makedirs("../data/raw", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs("../data/processed", exist_ok=True)

# download the zip file from the UCI Machine Learning Repository
url = "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/222/bank+marketing.zip"
zip_path = "../data/raw/bank+marketing.zip"

response = requests.get(url)
response.raise_for_status()  # stop with an error if the download failed
with open(zip_path, "wb") as f:
    f.write(response.content)

with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as z:
    z.extractall("../data/raw")

with zipfile.ZipFile("../data/raw/bank.zip") as z:
    z.extractall("../data/raw")
```

```{python}
# read in the full data set
bank = pd.read_csv("../data/raw/bank-full.csv", sep=";")
```

Before cleaning the data, we checked that the download was complete and that the file has no empty cells or duplicate rows (Table 1). These checks only confirm that the file was read correctly, so they do not use any information that could influence our modelling decisions.

Table 1. Basic checks of the full data set.

```{python}
pd.DataFrame({
    "Check": ["Number of rows", "Number of columns", "Empty cells", "Duplicate rows"],
    "Result": [
        bank.shape[0],
        bank.shape[1],
        bank.isna().sum().sum(),
        bank.duplicated().sum()
    ]
}).set_index("Check")
```

We removed the call duration variable before modelling. The duration of a call is only known after the call has ended, and by then the outcome (whether the client subscribed) is also known. A model that uses call duration therefore cannot help the bank decide which clients to call, which is the purpose of our analysis. This decision is based on the meaning of the variable, not on the data, so it is safe to make before splitting the data.

```{python}
# drop duration: it is only known after the call ends,
# so it cannot be used to predict before calling a client
bank_clean = bank.drop(columns=["duration"])
bank_clean.to_csv("../data/processed/bank_clean.csv", index=False)
```

We then split the data into a training set (80%) and a test set (20%). We split the data before any further exploration, so that the test set does not influence any decision we make. Because only a small share of clients subscribed to a term deposit, we used a stratified split, which keeps the same proportion of subscribers in both sets.

```{python}
# split the data into training (80%) and test (20%) sets
bank_train, bank_test = train_test_split(
    bank_clean,
    test_size=0.2,
    stratify=bank_clean["y"],
    random_state=522
)

bank_train.to_csv("../data/processed/bank_train.csv", index=False)
bank_test.to_csv("../data/processed/bank_test.csv", index=False)
```

## Data quality in the training set

Although the data set has no empty cells, some categorical variables record missing information as the value "unknown" (Table 2). This affects four variables in the training set: job, education, contact type and the outcome of the previous campaign.

Table 2. Number and percentage of "unknown" values in the training set, for the variables that contain them.

```{python}
# count "unknown" values in each column of the training set
unknown_counts = (bank_train == "unknown").sum()
unknown_counts = unknown_counts[unknown_counts > 0]

unknown_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Number of unknown values": unknown_counts,
    "Percent of training rows": (unknown_counts / len(bank_train) * 100).round(1)
}).rename(index={
    "job": "Job",
    "education": "Education",
    "contact": "Contact type",
    "poutcome": "Previous campaign outcome"
})
unknown_table.index.name = "Variable"
unknown_table
```

To understand the "unknown" values in the previous campaign outcome, we compared this variable with the number of days since the client was last contacted in a previous campaign. The data set uses -1 for clients who were not previously contacted (Table 3).

Table 3. Number of clients in the training set with an unknown previous campaign outcome, and how many of them were not previously contacted.

```{python}
# keep only the clients whose previous campaign outcome is "unknown"
unknown_poutcome = bank_train[bank_train["poutcome"] == "unknown"]

# count how many of them were not previously contacted (pdays == -1)
n_unknown = len(unknown_poutcome)
n_not_contacted = (unknown_poutcome["pdays"] == -1).sum()

pd.DataFrame({
    "Clients with unknown previous outcome": [n_unknown],
    "Of these, not previously contacted": [n_not_contacted],
    "Percent not previously contacted": [round(n_not_contacted / n_unknown * 100, 2)]
}, index=["Training set"])
```

Almost all clients with an unknown previous campaign outcome (29,563 of 29,567, or 99.99%) were not contacted in a previous campaign (Table 3). For this variable, "unknown" therefore does not represent missing information: it means that there was no previous campaign for that client. For the other three variables, the "unknown" values are true missing information, but we kept them as well. Removing these rows would discard a large part of the data, because almost a third of the clients in the training set have an unknown contact type (Table 2). We therefore kept "unknown" as its own category in all four variables, so that the model can learn from it like any other category.

### Binary features
To look at whether the categorical and binary features are useful to predict term deposit subscription, we plot the features as bar charts. The pattern we want to find is whether subscription differed for different levels of the same category and if it differed, then by how much. 
For that, we calculate the subscription rate in each category for its respective levels and compare those rates in the bar chart. We divide it into 3 faceted bar charts; one for binary features, one for categorical features with 3/4 categories and the other for categorical features
with more than 4 categories. From Figure 2, we can see prev_contacted has a stronger signal than the others, with around 15 percentage points more subscription rate if the client was contacted before compared to a first contact. Housing also has a good signal with a difference of around
10 percentage points more subscription rate among clients that don't have a housing loan compared to the clients who do. 

```{python}
def subscription_rate(df, col):
    return(
        df.assign(subscribed=(df["y"]=="yes"))
        .groupby(col)["subscribed"].mean()
        .reset_index(name="rate")
    )

bank_train_eda = bank_train.assign(prev_contacted = (bank_train["pdays"]!= -1))

bi_cols = ["housing", "loan", "default", "prev_contacted"]

bi_perc = []

for col in bi_cols:
    r = subscription_rate(bank_train_eda, col).rename(columns = {col:"category"})
    r ["feature"] = col
    bi_perc.append(r)

rates_bi = pd.concat(bi_perc, ignore_index=True)

bi_chart = (
    alt.Chart(rates_bi)
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("rate:Q", title = "Subscription rate", axis=alt.Axis(format="%")),
        y=alt.Y("category:N", sort = "-x", title = None)
        )
    .properties(width=130, height=100)
    .facet(facet="feature:N", columns=2)
    .resolve_scale(y="independent")
    .properties(title = alt.TitleParams(
        text="Binary features with Subscription rate",
        anchor="middle"))
    )

bi_chart
```
**Figure 2.** Comparison of term deposit subscription rate between binary features of training data


### Categorical features
Next, let's look at categorical features with 3/4 levels. Among those 4 categories, it is evident from Figure 3 that for marital, contact, and education, the subscription rate doesn't vary that much across levels. But for previous campaign outcome (poutcome), the subscription rate for clients 
who were also a success in the previous campaign is much higher compared to other levels. For categories with more than 4 levels (Figure 4), month also has higher subscription rate in the months of March, September, October and December. For jobs, an interesting finding is students who conventionally 
don't have a fixed income have the highest subscription rate among all the jobs. But the levels in job category don't vary by a large magnitude like poutcome, so signal from this category would be relatively weaker.

### Numeric features
Before analyzing the numeric features, we want to note that from the descriptive summary, it looks like two of the numeric features are right skewed where mean is way above the median (balance and campaign) so, we are plotting the numeric features as boxplots
to understand the skewness of the data and to see if the numeric data (namely the median and IQR) behave differently for people who subscribe compared to people who didn't. So, from Figure 6 below, we can see that medians across all 4 numeric features are 
nearly the same for both subscribers and non subscribers. The IQRs for all 4 features also have a lot of overlap which means that the numeric features are weaker signals compared to the categorical features. Two features worth mentioning are campaign and balance. 
From campaign feature (the number of contacts during this campaign), we can see that the subscribers tend to have fewer contacts compared to non subscribers. That means making more contacts with a potential client doesn't necessarily convert them. The ones that subscribe, 
tend to do so without needing a lot of followups or contacts. Moreover, the balance features show that subscribers tend to have higher balances, and negative balances are rare among them.

## Analysis
The Python programming language (Van Rossum and Drake 2009) and the following Python packages were used to perform the analysis: requests (Reitz 2011), zipfile (Van Rossum and Drake 2009), NumPy (Harris et al. 2020), pandas (McKinney 2010), Altair (VanderPlas et al. 2018) and scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). The code used to perform the analysis and create this report can be found here: <https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/DSCI-522-GROUP-6-Predicting_term_deposit_subscription>.

First, we examined the features based on their definitions and relevance to predicting term deposit subscriptions. The duration feature represents the duration of the last contact with a client, measured in seconds. Since this information is only available after a call has taken place, including it would introduce data leakage when predicting whether a client will subscribe before making the call. Therefore, we excluded duration from the analysis. 

Second, we divided the features into three main categories: numerical, categorical, and binary. Binary features can be represented in different formats, such as 0 and 1 or "yes" and "no". These features were identified and processed according to their data types and meanings.

One feature requiring special attention was pdays, which represents the number of days since a client was last contacted during a previous campaign. A value of -1 indicates that the client had not been previously contacted, while non-negative values indicate the number of days since the previous contact. Since -1 has a different meaning from non-negative values, treating all values as ordinary numerical observations would be inappropriate. Additionally, most observations had a value of -1. Therefore, we transformed pdays into a new binary feature called previously_contacted, where -1 was encoded as 0 and all non-negative values were encoded as 1. This transformation distinguishes clients who had been previously contacted from those who had not, although it removes information about the exact number of days since the previous contact.

```{python}
X_train = bank_train.drop(columns="y")
y_train = bank_train["y"]

X_test = bank_test.drop(columns="y")
y_test = bank_test["y"]

def transform_pdays(X):
    X = X.copy()
    X["previously_contacted"] = (X["pdays"] != -1).astype(int)
    return X.drop(columns=["pdays"])

numeric_features = ["age", "balance", "day", "campaign", "previous"]
categorical_features = ["job", "marital", "education", "contact", "poutcome"]
binary_features = ["default", "housing", "loan"]
contacted_features = ["previously_contacted"]
```

```{python}
numeric_pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler())

categorical_pipe = make_pipeline(OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))

binary_pipe = make_pipeline(OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["no", "yes"]] * len(binary_features)))

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("numeric", numeric_pipe, numeric_features),
        ("categorical", categorical_pipe, categorical_features),
        ("binary", binary_pipe, binary_features),
        ("contacted", "passthrough", contacted_features)
    ],
    remainder="drop",
    verbose_feature_names_out=False
)

full_preprocessor = make_pipeline(
    FunctionTransformer(transform_pdays, validate=False),
    preprocessor
)

X_train_processed = full_preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_processed = full_preprocessor.transform(X_test)
```

For model training, we decide to take the Dummy Classifier as the baseline. And then we are going to set Logistic Regression and KNearestNeighbour as 2 candidates. All of the three models are trained with the same condition, which is 5-fold cross-validation. 

As the DummyClassifier Model Result (Table .) shown below, the DummyClassifier achieved a validation accuracy of 0.883, while the f1 score is 0, which indicates that this model failed to identify customers who subscribed to a term deposit. This is might because of the class imbalance in the dataset.

Table. DummyClassifier Model Result
```{python}
dummy_pipe = make_pipeline(
    full_preprocessor,
    DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")
)

cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=123
)

scoring = {
    "accuracy": "accuracy",
    "precision": make_scorer(precision_score, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0),
    "recall": make_scorer(recall_score, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0),
    "f1": make_scorer(f1_score, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0)
}

dummy_scores = cross_validate(
    dummy_pipe,
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cv=cv,
    scoring=scoring,
    return_train_score=True
)

dummy_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": ["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"],
    "Train": [
        dummy_scores["train_accuracy"].mean(),
        dummy_scores["train_precision"].mean(),
        dummy_scores["train_recall"].mean(),
        dummy_scores["train_f1"].mean()
    ],
    "Validation": [
        dummy_scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        dummy_scores["test_precision"].mean(),
        dummy_scores["test_recall"].mean(),
        dummy_scores["test_f1"].mean()
    ]
})

display(dummy_results.round(3))
```

As the Logistic Regression Model Result (Table ) shown below, we can see that Logistic Regression gets validation accuracy as 0.894, precision as 0.676, recall as 0.174, and F1 score as 0.277. We can see all of the data is higher than DummyClassifier model. This indicates that this model is a better choice compared with DummyClassifier model. Low reecall is one problem of Logistic Regression model. This means the model correctly identified only about 17.4% of customers who actually subscribed to a term deposit, missing approximately 82.6% of potential subscribers. It suggests that the model is relatively conservative when predicting the positive class. One possible reason is the class imbalance in the dataset, which may cause the model to favor the majority class. To improve recall, we could explore using class_weight="balanced" or adjusting the classification threshold, although these changes may reduce precision.

Table. Logistic Regression Model Result
```{python}
reg_pipe = make_pipeline(
    full_preprocessor,
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=123)
)

reg_scores = cross_validate(
    reg_pipe,
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cv=cv,
    scoring=scoring,
    return_train_score=True
)

reg_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": ["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"],
    "Train": [
        reg_scores["train_accuracy"].mean(),
        reg_scores["train_precision"].mean(),
        reg_scores["train_recall"].mean(),
        reg_scores["train_f1"].mean()
    ],
    "Validation": [
        reg_scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        reg_scores["test_precision"].mean(),
        reg_scores["test_recall"].mean(),
        reg_scores["test_f1"].mean()
    ]
})

display(reg_results.round(3))
```

As the KNearestNeighbour (KNN) Model Result (Table .) shown below, we can see that KNN model gets accuracy as 0.884, precision as 0.506, recall as 0.192, F1 score as 0.278. All of the present data is also better than DummyClassifier model. This indicates that this model is better than DummyClassifier model.

Table. KNearestNeighbour (KNN) Model Result
```{python}
knn_pipe = make_pipeline(
    full_preprocessor,
    KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
)

knn_scores = cross_validate(
    knn_pipe,
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cv=cv,
    scoring=scoring,
    return_train_score=True
)

knn_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": ["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"],
    "Train": [
        knn_scores["train_accuracy"].mean(),
        knn_scores["train_precision"].mean(),
        knn_scores["train_recall"].mean(),
        knn_scores["train_f1"].mean()
    ],
    "Validation": [
        knn_scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        knn_scores["test_precision"].mean(),
        knn_scores["test_recall"].mean(),
        knn_scores["test_f1"].mean()
    ]
})

display(knn_results.round(3))
```


As the Conclusion of data from three models (Table .) shown below, in comparison of Logistic Regression and KNearestNeighbour, we can find that the gap of f1 score of train and validation of Logistic Regression, which is about 0.01, is much smaller than the one of K-Nearest Neighbour model, which is about 0.12. This indicates that KNN model is might a bit overfitting. However, improving recall remains an important direction for future model development.

Table.  Conclusion of data from three models
```{python}
comparison_df = pd.concat([
    dummy_results.assign(Model="Dummy"),
    reg_results.assign(Model="Logistic Regression"),
    knn_results.assign(Model="KNN")
], ignore_index=True)

display(comparison_df.round(3))
```

Therefore, we still want to choose the Logistic Regression as the best model to use, because it provides comparable validation F1 performance and higher precision.
